Molecular Toxicity Prediction via Fingerprints and Molecular Graph Networks¶

AML / DL Group Project 8: Tox21, 12 toxicity endpoints¶

Question. Do learned molecular-graph representations (message passing neural networks) predict toxicity-assay activity better than engineered chemical fingerprints, especially on chemical families never seen in training?

Approach (the "hybrid" logic).

  1. AML baseline: SMILES → Morgan fingerprints (ECFP4, 2048 bits) + 200+ RDKit descriptors → one Logistic Regression / Random Forest / XGBoost model per endpoint.
  2. Gap: fingerprints encode a fixed dictionary of circular substructures. They cannot adapt to the endpoint, and they do not share information across the 12 related assays.
  3. DL model: graph neural networks where atoms are nodes and bonds are edges (GCN, GINE message passing with bond features, AttentiveFP), trained multitask with a masked loss so missing labels contribute nothing. We add two controls: an FP-MLP (same fingerprints, deep multitask) and a Hybrid (graph embedding + fingerprint).
  4. Fair comparison: identical cleaned data, identical scaffold splits (3 seeds), train-only preprocessing, validation-only model selection, and endpoint-wise ROC-AUC and PR-AUC that exclude missing labels. The same models are also run on random splits to measure the scaffold generalisation gap.

Everything below is reproducible with ./run_all.sh. This notebook reads the saved results and regenerates every table and figure.

1. Data preparation¶

Source: Tox21 from MoleculeNet / DeepChem (tox21.csv.gz): 7,831 rows, 12 binary endpoints (7 nuclear-receptor NR-* assays and 5 stress-response SR-* assays).

Step What we do Why
Parse RDKit MolFromSmiles, drop unparseable rows invalid structures cannot be featurised
Standardise RDKit cleanup → keep the largest organic fragment → canonical SMILES strips salts and counter-ions so the same parent compound has one identity
Deduplicate before splitting group by canonical SMILES. Agreeing labels are merged, conflicting labels become missing prevents the same molecule appearing in both train and test (leakage)
Missing labels kept as NaN → boolean mask ~17% of labels are missing. We never impute them as negatives
Scaffolds Bemis–Murcko scaffold per molecule used for scaffold splitting

The endpoints are heavily imbalanced (2–16% actives). This is why we (i) weight the positive class endpoint by endpoint (class_weight='balanced' / scale_pos_weight for the baselines, pos_weight in the masked BCE for the networks) and (ii) report PR-AUC next to ROC-AUC. PR-AUC is sensitive to performance on the rare positive class, and its chance level equals the prevalence.

2. Scaffold splitting: testing on unseen chemical families¶

A random split puts close analogues of training molecules into the test set, which inflates scores. We use a randomised Bemis–Murcko scaffold split (80/10/10). Every scaffold group is assigned to exactly one partition, so test molecules come from ring systems the model has never seen. Large groups (acyclic molecules, benzene) are forced into train so they do not dominate the small test sets. Three seeds give three different, equally strict splits. We report mean ± std over them.

3. Models¶

3.1 AML baselines (engineered features, one model per endpoint)¶

  • Features: Morgan/ECFP4 fingerprint (radius 2, 2048 bits) plus all RDKit 2D descriptors. Descriptors get a signed-log transform, median imputation and standardisation fitted on the training split only.
  • Models: Logistic Regression (L2, C grid), Random Forest (500 trees, leaf/feature grid), XGBoost (depth/column-sampling grid, early stopping on validation).
  • For each endpoint only molecules with an observed label are used. Hyper-parameters are chosen by validation ROC-AUC, and the test set is touched once.
  • Ablation: XGBoost on fingerprints only (XGBoost-FPonly) isolates the value of the descriptors.

3.2 DL models (multitask, masked loss)¶

  • Graph: 56-d atom features (element, degree, charge, hybridisation, #H, chirality, aromaticity, ring, mass) and 12-d bond features (type, stereo, conjugation, ring). Edges are bidirectional.
  • GCN: 4 graph-convolution layers with residuals and batch-norm, mean+max readout.
  • GINE-MPNN: 4 GIN layers whose messages are conditioned on bond features, sum+mean readout.
  • AttentiveFP: attention-based message passing plus a GRU graph readout (Xiong et al., 2019).
  • FP-MLP (control): same engineered features as the AML models, but a deep multitask network.
  • Hybrid (end-to-end): GINE-MPNN graph embedding concatenated with the fingerprint/descriptor vector. A naive version early-stopped after 3–30 epochs because the fingerprint branch memorises the training set long before the graph branch learns (val ROC-AUC 0.78, below either component). The final version uses input dropout, a narrow projection, stronger L2 on the fingerprint branch, and modality dropout (the fingerprint embedding is zeroed for a random 50% of training molecules), which moved the best epoch to ~60 and raised val ROC-AUC on scaffold seed 0 from 0.784 to 0.829.
  • Ensemble RF+GNN (late fusion): per endpoint, a rank-average of Random Forest and the graph model with the best validation ROC-AUC on that split. The mixing weight w ∈ {0, .25, .5, .75, 1} is chosen on validation.
  • All networks: 12 sigmoid outputs, AdamW, early stopping on mean validation ROC-AUC, LR decay on plateau.

Masked loss. Missing labels are excluded from the loss. Positive-class weights are computed per endpoint from the training labels:

In [6]:
print(inspect.getsource(gnn.masked_bce))

def masked_bce(logits, y, pos_weight):
    """BCE over observed labels only; NaN labels contribute nothing."""
    mask = ~torch.isnan(y)
    y0 = torch.nan_to_num(y, nan=0.0)
    loss = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits, y0, pos_weight=pos_weight, reduction="none")
    return (loss * mask).sum() / mask.sum().clamp(min=1)

5. Scaffold generalisation analysis¶

Three complementary views:

  1. Random vs scaffold split: how much each model's ROC-AUC drops when the test chemistry is new.
  2. Per-endpoint gap: which assays are hardest to extrapolate.
  3. Accuracy vs distance to the training set: each test molecule is binned by the Tanimoto similarity to its nearest training neighbour (test sets of all 6 splits pooled).

6. Discussion¶

6.1 Do learned graph representations beat engineered fingerprints?¶

Not on their own, at this data scale. On scaffold splits the best single model is the fingerprint + descriptor Random Forest (ROC-AUC 0.834 ± 0.033, PR-AUC 0.496 ± 0.054). It is significantly better than every graph network (paired Wilcoxon over 36 endpoint × seed pairs: vs GCN +0.017, p = 0.004; vs AttentiveFP +0.017, p = 0.0001; vs GINE-MPNN +0.031, p = 0.0001). The best graph networks (GCN 0.817, AttentiveFP 0.818) are statistically indistinguishable from XGBoost (0.816) and from the FP-MLP (0.814) (all p > 0.3). The gap the brief hypothesised, that fixed substructure dictionaries miss task-specific interactions, is real but small. About 6k training molecules are not enough for message passing to learn a representation clearly better than ECFP4 plus 217 curated physicochemical descriptors. This agrees with MoleculeNet (Wu et al., 2018) and Chemprop (Yang et al., 2019), where graph models only pull clearly ahead of fingerprints on larger datasets or with pre-training.

6.2 But the two representations are complementary¶

  • Graph models win individual endpoints that fingerprints handle poorly. NR-Aromatase is best with GCN (0.804 vs 0.750 for RF). AttentiveFP is the best single model on NR-PPAR-gamma (0.875 vs 0.870).
  • The late-fusion ensemble RF+GNN is the best model overall: ROC-AUC 0.844 ± 0.025, PR-AUC 0.503 ± 0.033 on scaffold splits. It beats RF alone on 26 of 36 endpoint × seed pairs (p = 0.001) and is best on 8 of 12 endpoints for ROC-AUC and on 7 of 12 for PR-AUC. The mixing weights, chosen on validation only, put on average 0.46 of the weight on the graph model. If the GNN carried no information beyond the fingerprint, these weights would collapse to 0.
  • End-to-end fusion is harder than late fusion. Even after the modality-dropout fix, the joint Hybrid network (0.809) does not beat its components. The two branches learn at very different speeds (see the learning curves: the FP-MLP's training loss collapses within 10 epochs while the graph models need 40–90), so a single early-stopping point is a compromise for both.

6.3 Scaffold generalisation¶

  • The scaffold split is the honest test. Every model scores lower on scaffold splits than on random splits (Fig. 5–6). Under random splitting the median test molecule has a Tanimoto similarity of 0.58 to its nearest training molecule, against 0.45 under scaffold splitting. 7.1% of random-split test molecules have a fingerprint identical to a training molecule (mostly stereoisomers, which are different canonical SMILES but have the same non-chiral ECFP), against 0.4% for scaffold splits.
  • Graph networks lose more when the chemistry is new. The random → scaffold drop is 0.028–0.030 ROC-AUC for GCN, GINE-MPNN and AttentiveFP, but only 0.014 for RF and 0.016 for XGBoost. On random splits GCN (0.847) and AttentiveFP (0.847) tie RF (0.849). So part of the GNNs' apparent strength on random splits comes from interpolating between close analogues, which a scaffold split removes.
  • Accuracy versus distance to the training set (Fig. 7). All models are good on molecules with a close training neighbour (Tanimoto ≥ 0.7: ROC-AUC 0.85–0.88) and degrade sharply for genuinely novel chemistry (< 0.3: 0.64–0.72). In that hardest bin RF (0.718) and GINE-MPNN (0.706) hold up best among single models, XGBoost degrades most (0.637), and the ensemble is best (0.723). This is the practically relevant regime for screening new chemical series, and no model is reliable there.
  • Endpoint level. The stress-response assays (SR-ARE, SR-ATAD5, SR-MMP, SR-p53) and NR-AhR / NR-Aromatase have the largest scaffold gaps (≈ 0.055–0.068 averaged over models). They are driven by scaffold-specific chemotypes, so they are harder to extrapolate. NR-ER and NR-AR show negative gaps, which reflects the high variance of their small positive sets across splits rather than easier extrapolation.

6.4 Other observations¶

  • Descriptors matter as much as the model. XGBoost on fingerprints only reaches 0.751, against 0.816 with descriptors added. Global properties such as logP, molecular weight and charge are strong toxicity signals that a GNN must learn from scratch from atom-level features.
  • More expressive is not better here. The bond-aware GINE-MPNN is significantly worse than the plain GCN (−0.014, p = 0.007) and has the lowest PR-AUC of the graph models. Its extra capacity overfits the small training set.
  • Split variance is larger than most model differences. The standard deviation across the three scaffold seeds (0.02–0.04) exceeds most pairwise model gaps. A single-split comparison could easily rank the models differently, which is why we report mean ± std and use paired tests.
  • PR-AUC tells a harsher story than ROC-AUC. For rare endpoints (SR-ATAD5 at 4% prevalence, NR-PPAR-gamma at 3%) PR-AUC stays at 0.2–0.37 even when ROC-AUC exceeds 0.84. Ranking actives first is still hard, which matters for prioritising compounds for wet-lab testing.

6.5 Limitations and future work¶

  • The baselines got a per-endpoint grid search, while the networks used one fixed architecture and setting each. A larger GNN search might narrow the gap.
  • No self-supervised pre-training on large unlabelled molecule sets (e.g. GROVER, pretrained GIN). This is the most promising route to make graph representations beat fingerprints at this data size.
  • Three seeds per split type; uncertainty estimates would tighten with more.
  • Class-weighted losses optimise ranking, not calibration. Probabilities would need recalibration (e.g. Platt / isotonic on the validation set) before being used as risk scores.
  • Eight SMILES that newer RDKit versions reject were dropped. Stereoisomers were kept as separate compounds.

7. Conclusion¶

On Tox21 under a strict scaffold split, engineered fingerprints plus descriptors with a Random Forest remain the strongest single model. Message passing networks are competitive with XGBoost and a deep fingerprint MLP but do not surpass them, and they degrade more when moving to unseen scaffolds. However, the graph models capture complementary information: a validation-weighted late fusion of RF and a GNN is the best model overall (scaffold ROC-AUC 0.844, PR-AUC 0.503) and wins most endpoints. In this low-data regime the practical recommendation is to combine engineered and learned representations, not to replace one with the other.
